title: $ 57.5 m boost for rooftop solar, net metering | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 5 October 2026 04:56
-     - 11

The Government of Sri Lanka has signed an agreement with the Asian Development Bank (ADB) to secure a concessional loan of $ 35 million from ADB, together with a grant of Euro 15.4 million from the European Union (EU) (equivalent to $ 16.94 million) and a grant of $ 5.5 million from the Japan Fund for the Joint Crediting Mechanism (JFJCM).

The Energy Ministry in collaboration with Electricity Distribution Lanka Ltd., (EDL) and Lanka Electricity Company Ltd., (LECO), will implement the project from 2026 to 2030 in support of the Government’s efforts to expand access to affordable clean energy

Under the project, EDL’s CEBAssist solution will be enhanced with an Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI) system. a Distributed Energy Resource Management (DERM) system, and distribution control centres supported by an Advanced Distribution Management System (ADMS). These systems will digitalise EDL’s customer and operational services and improve network reliability by enabling faster restoration of supply after outages. The smart meters and supporting infrastructure will also provide the real-time visibility and control needed to expand the use of renewable energy and extend the benefits of solar power to more people. EDL will thereby establish a more efficient, reliable and sustainable smart grid.

The project will also introduce Virtual Net Metering (VNM) to Sri Lanka for the first time. Funded by an EU grant, 25 MW of aggregated rooftop solar PV will be used to reduce the electricity bill burden on the country’s small and medium- scale entrepreneurs. These plants will be equipped with state-of-the-art control capability, allowing the National System Operator to manage their generation in line with prevailing network constraints.

Within LECO’s service area, in addition to the VNM scheme, low-loss conductors will be installed to improve the efficiency of the distribution network. High-capacity battery energy storage systems installed at distribution transformer level will increase the network’s renewable energy hosting capacity and provide much-needed controllability over renewable energy management. With a particular focus on the Negombo area, LECO expects to enhance its network capacity to connect more high-capacity commercial and industrial loads, while strengthening the network to absorb higher levels of renewable energy and improving the flexibility, resilience and reliability of supply.

The relevant loan and grant agreements were signed at the General Treasury on 1 October by Treasury Secretary Dr. Harshana Suriyapperuma,  on behalf of the Government of Sri Lanka, and ADB Country Director Shannon Cowlin, on behalf of the ADB in the presence of the Delegation of the European Union to Sri Lanka Head of Partnerships Virginie Laffeur-Tighe and Embassy of Japan Deputy Chief of Mission (Minister) Naoki Kamoshida.

title: From wetlands to wellbeing: Sri Lanka explores new tourism frontier via global conference on 9 Oct. | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 5 October 2026 04:55
-     - 8

As tourism increasingly moves beyond conventional leisure experiences, Sri Lanka is seeking to turn its rich wetland ecosystems into destinations for wellness, conservation and community-based economic activity, with an international summit opening in Kotte on 9 October.

The Wellness in Wetlands International Conference (WIWC) 2026), scheduled from 9 to 12 October in the historic Kingdom of Kotte, will bring together 34 international experts from 15 countries, including environmental psychologists, ecologists, ecotourism specialists, indigenous knowledge holders and community leaders.

Organised by the Emotional Intelligence and Life Skills Training Team Ltd., the conference is expected to provide a platform to examine how wetland conservation can be integrated with nature-based wellness and tourism development.

The international participation this year extends beyond Asia, with experts from Mexico and Kenya joining the program.

The initiative comes as Sri Lanka continues to diversify its tourism products, with wellness and nature-based tourism emerging as areas with potential to attract higher-value visitors while supporting environmental conservation and local communities.

WIWC 2026 will focus particularly on developing models that connect wetland ecosystem preservation with mental and planetary health. The organisers also see youth development as a key component, with the conference expected to explore ways of equipping young people with life skills and knowledge to participate in nature-based wellness initiatives and the wider green economy.

The conference is being organised in collaboration with SriLankan Airlines, the Sri Lanka Tourism Promotion Bureau (SLTPB), the Professional Wetlands Guides Association and the Kotte Green Tourism Network.

It has also received official backing from the Ministry of Environment and the Ministry of Trade, Commerce, Food Security, and Co-operative Development.

The organisers said the selection of Kotte as the venue would highlight the relationship between Sri Lanka’s historical heritage and its wetland ecosystems, while drawing attention to the tourism potential of wetlands within and around the capital.

The program will bring together stakeholders from the tourism, hospitality, environmental, wellness and research sectors, with the organisers inviting local entrepreneurs, practitioners and young leaders to participate.

The conference is expected to explore how Sri Lanka could develop new tourism experiences around its natural ecosystems without compromising conservation objectives.

With international wellness tourism increasingly moving towards experiences that combine nature, health and cultural engagement, WIWC 2026 seeks to position Sri Lanka’s wetlands as an asset not only for biodiversity conservation but also for wellbeing, sustainable tourism and community-based economic development.

title: AAT Sri Lanka Conference 2026 explores competence, credibility and professional power | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 5 October 2026 04:51
-     - 11

AAT Sri Lanka President Dr. Chamara Bandara (second from left) presents a memento to keynote speaker CA Sri Lanka President Tishan Subasinghe. Others from left: AAT Sri Lanka CEO Tishanga Kumarasinghe, Vice President Dayal Abhayasinghe, Chief Operating Officer Himali Dasanayake and Conference Committee Chairman Isuru Kalhara

CA Sri Lanka President Tishan Subasinghe delivering the keynote

The AAT Sri Lanka Conference 2026 examined how knowledge, character and continued performance translate into professional influence, with keynote speaker CA Sri Lanka President Tishan Subasinghe addressing the conference theme “Precision of Power.”

Held on 8 and 9 September at Waters Edge, Battaramulla, the conference brought together industry leaders and professionals for two days centred on knowledge, collaboration and the future of the accounting profession.

At the request of the conference chairperson, Subasinghe set aside technical subject matter and built his address around the two elements of the theme: power and precision.

“Precision turns knowledge into competency; competency builds credibility; credibility creates influence; and influence over a period of time gives power — not mere authority or designation,” he said.

His central message was that power does not create character; it reveals it. “If you want to see the true nature and colours of a person, put them in a seat with authority and power,” he told delegates.

Sources of professional power

Subasinghe described power as the ability, strength or right to act, control people, get things done and influence people and processes. He noted that power is often tied to position, authority and seniority, with seniority frequently outweighing talent in this part of the world.

Turning to accountants and business leaders, he identified knowledge, technological ability, networks, relationships, communication and execution skills as sources of professional power.

“Knowledge is power. Technological ability is power. Networks and relationships are power. Communication skills and execution skills are sources of power,” he said. “If one cannot get things executed, there is no power; people notice, and you cannot lead.”

Calling power “a dangerous game,” he traced the concept through history, referring to Chanakya during the Maurya Empire and Niccolò Machiavelli in Italy, who had counselled rulers on acquiring and retaining power.

“On a daily basis, politicians go to jail because of power, people kill and get killed because of power, and kings wage war because of power. In corporate boardrooms, board chairpersons are taken out and replaced, all for power,” he said.

He cautioned that power requires careful use. “As much as power is beautiful, useful and resourceful, unless it is put to correct use, the person holding power opens the doors to destruction.”

Precision through credibility and performance

Comparing power to a baked cake and precision to its icing, Subasinghe described precision as the disciplined positioning of power as something earned rather than assumed.

“Precision is positioning power as something earned through knowledge, character, credibility, relationships and continued performance,” he said.

Promoting people into authority before they have developed those attributes, he warned, “can create a mess within an organisation.”

At the chairperson’s request, he illustrated the theme through his career, beginning with his early years at BDO across audit, forensic investigation, due diligence, valuation and information systems work.

“On my first valuation report 15 years ago, I received a five-to-six-page letter from the Securities and Exchange Commission highlighting mistakes,” he recalled. “Through hard work on assignments for companies like the Tata Group, I learned until we reached a point where we received no negative comments.”

He said consistent preparation earned him rapid promotions while working with PwC’s Southern African practice. Recalling an audit of a large garment manufacturer in Botswana employing between 5,000 and 6,000 workers, he described how refusing a bribe strengthened his credibility.

“I uncovered a fraud. The directors offered bribes to conceal it, but I reported it to my partners at PwC. When law enforcement investigated, the directors acknowledged that I had refused the money. That credibility opened opportunities for me to work at PwC’s international head office in Manhattan, New York.”

He also discussed his work on Sarbanes-Oxley compliance in the United States, where he later qualified as an Attorney-at-Law. Combining accounting, auditing and legal knowledge, he said, “allows us to produce unique reports that provide true precision to power.”

Sustained professional relationships and communication, he added, contributed to his election as President of CA Sri Lanka.

Connecting the conference themes to practice

Closing his address, Subasinghe stressed that knowledge becomes power only when applied. He cited his MBA studies, which he said he extended from 25 academic modules into 33 applied areas, including transforming non-billing functions such as human resources into revenue-generating consulting work.

He linked this approach directly to the AAT Sri Lanka Conference programme.

“The segments of this conference directly align with building precision: business and entrepreneurial thinking, tax and technical knowledge, technology and AI, and understanding people and leadership,” he said.

“By updating yourself across these themes, you put the icing on the cake, stay relevant, and draw the required energy to seize power in your organisations.”

title: HayWind commences turbine tower erection at Mannar wind farm | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 5 October 2026 04:49
-     - 11

Heavy lifting operations underway as the HayWind nacelle is positioned atop the tower at the Mannar site

HayWind One Ltd., the wind energy arm of Hayleys Fentons Ltd., has marked a major milestone in the development of its 50MW Mannar Wind Farm, with turbine installation now in full swing and the first two 5MW wind turbines fully erected. The milestone sets the pace for the continuous installation of all ten turbines across the utility-scale project.

Each complete wind turbine reaches an impressive tip height of approximately 186.5 metres. The structure comprises a 110-metre tower assembled in four sections anchored to a heavy-duty concrete foundation reinforced with piles, an anchor cage, foundation bolts, and a high-strength grout layer. Mounted atop the tower is the nacelle, housing the main bearing, drive shaft, gearbox, generator, and an active yaw system to keep the rotor aligned with prevailing winds fitted with the hub and three 76.5-metre rotor blades. Given Mannar’s coastal conditions, all turbine components are equipped with specialised marine-grade anti-corrosion coatings and filtration systems.

The heavy lifting operations are carried out using a massive 900-tonne crawler crane, the largest ever deployed for a wind energy project in Sri Lanka supplied by Hayleys Advantis Limited in partnership with Sarans India. Prior to positioning the crane, engineering teams executed extensive ground stabilization, including aggregate base course preparation, soil compaction, and rigorous load-bearing tests to ensure platform safety.

Managing Director Hasith Prematillake said: “Seeing our initial turbines fully erected in Mannar is a defining milestone for HayWind and a clear testament to what our engineering capabilities can achieve. Executing installations of this sheer scale requires meticulous planning, seamless cross-functional coordination, and high-calibre technical expertise. With the first turbines now standing tall, our teams have established strong operational momentum to deliver the remaining units.”

Deputy Managing Director Roshane Perera added: “Turbine erection at this scale demands uncompromising safety standards, technical competence, and disciplined execution. Our engineers, site supervisors, and technical crews are GWO-certified (Global Wind Organisation), ensuring all operations strictly adhere to globally benchmarked protocols for wind energy construction.”

HayWind One COO Prashantha Amarasinghe said: “Each lift is executed around dynamic ground and atmospheric conditions, strictly limited to wind speeds of 9.8 metres per second or below in compliance with OEM parameters. Ground stability and wind profiles are validated prior to every lift. Heavy-duty taglines ensure lateral control of each section during hoisting, complemented by real-time visual wind indicators to maintain precision.”

Upon completion, the Mannar Wind Farm will comprise ten 5MW turbines delivering an aggregate capacity of 50MW. The plant is projected to supply approximately 207 million units (kWh) of clean electricity annually to the national grid under a 20-year Power Purchase Agreement (PPA), saving Sri Lanka an estimated Rs. 100 billion in foreign exchange on fossil fuel imports over its operating lifecycle.

With turbine installation advancing swiftly across the site, HayWind One remains firmly on schedule for commissioning and grid energisation by December 2026, marking another landmark stride in Sri Lanka’s clean energy transition.

title: She’s Mercedes arrives in Sri Lanka | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 5 October 2026 04:47
-     - 18

Mercedes-Benz  has announced the launch of She’s Mercedes in Sri Lanka, introducing an exclusive community designed to celebrate, connect, and inspire women who shape industries, communities, and culture. 

The platform makes its Sri Lankan debut in conjunction with Mercedes-Benz Fashion Week Sri Lanka 2026, taking place from 7 to 11 October at Cinnamon Life, Colombo.

Rooted in the belief that luxury extends far beyond the automobile, She’s Mercedes embodies the values that have defined Mercedes-Benz for generations: excellence, confidence, innovation, and meaningful human connection. More than a platform, it is a global movement that brings together extraordinary women through shared experiences, compelling conversations, and opportunities to create lasting impact.

First established in 2015, She’s Mercedes has evolved into an international community spanning more than 70 countries. Its inspiration can be traced to Bertha Benz, whose pioneering journey in 1888 became one of the defining moments in automotive history. Her courage, vision, and determination transformed a revolutionary invention into a global phenomenon, laying the foundation for a legacy that continues to inspire women around the world. The philosophy remains as relevant today as it was then: when women move forward, they move the world forward.

In Sri Lanka, She’s Mercedes will serve as a private and thoughtfully curated circle for women who lead across business, entrepreneurship, design, technology, finance, academia, public service, and the social sector. It will provide a trusted environment where ambitions are shared, ideas are exchanged, and meaningful relationships are built among a community united by a commitment to excellence.

Throughout the year, members will be invited to intimate gatherings centered on topics that matter most to modern leaders, from building enduring enterprises and navigating transformation, to personal wellbeing, wealth creation, and purposeful living. Each gathering will be complemented by unique Mercedes-Benz experiences, including exclusive drive programmes, vehicle model previews, and curated luxury encounters. The annual calendar culminates at Mercedes-Benz Fashion Week Sri Lanka, where new members are welcomed and collective initiatives that support and empower women in Sri Lanka are championed.

Membership is exclusively reserved for women who own and drive a Mercedes-Benz vehicle purchased from DIMO, creating a community bound not only by achievement, but by a shared appreciation for one of the world’s most admired luxury brands.

The inaugural gathering will take place as an invitation-only luncheon on Saturday, 10 October, at the Mercedes-Benz Lounge at Cinnamon Life. At the heart of the occasion will be an inspiring dialogue exploring leadership, reinvention, resilience, and momentum.

DIMO Executive Director Rajeev Pandithage said: “For more than eight decades, DIMO has had the privilege of representing Mercedes-Benz in Sri Lanka and serving generations of discerning customers who share the brand’s appreciation for excellence. She’s Mercedes creates a meaningful platform for the remarkable women within this community, bringing together leadership, inspiration, and genuine connection. By connecting women across industries and generations, the initiative aims to spark new perspectives, encourage collaboration, and empower women to shape the future. It reflects the very essence of Mercedes-Benz: empowering individuals to pursue their ambitions with confidence while creating lasting impact.”

AOD Founder and Chairperson Linda Speldewinde said: “The story of Bertha Benz remains one of the most powerful examples of courage and belief in action. She chose to challenge convention, demonstrating what becomes possible when vision is paired with determination. Across Sri Lanka, countless women embody that same spirit as they build businesses, transform industries, and influence society. She’s Mercedes creates a platform where these journeys can be celebrated, where knowledge can be shared, and where future generations of women leaders can find inspiration and support. It is a natural extension of AOD’s commitment to elevating Sri Lankan creativity, talent, and leadership on the global stage.”

While launching during Mercedes-Benz Fashion Week Sri Lanka, She’s Mercedes is envisioned as a long-term platform that will continue to grow year after year. Through every gathering, conversation, and portrait, the community will become a living record of the women shaping contemporary Sri Lanka. More importantly, it will foster a powerful network built on shared values, mutual support, and the collective desire to create opportunities for those who follow.

From time to time, selected events will also welcome specially invited guests who embody the aspirations and values of the community. These women represent future connections, future collaborators, and potentially future members of the Mercedes-Benz family, enriching the platform through diverse perspectives and experiences.

title: Major General Milinda Peiris and KDU saga: Setting up university as task “Beyond Rank” | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 5 October 2026 04:00
-     - 140

General Sir John Kotelawala Defence University (KDU)

Though General Peiris was a seasoned soldier hardened by years in the field, he remained, above all else, an officer and a gentleman in the truest sense of the phrase. His approach to the highly volatile, real-world issues facing his fractured nation was characterised by an unyielding pragmatism and a strict commitment to rational analysis. He refused to allow emotional nationalism or rigid military dogma to cloud his judgment. This intellectual independence is starkly evident in the pioneering thesis he submitted to Madras University for his MPhil degree, appropriately titled ‘Political Reforms for Sustainable Peace in Sri Lanka’

Challenge of establishing a university

Establishing a university is a monumental undertaking that tests the limits of traditional leadership. The creation of a higher education institution requires a delicate synthesis of academic vision, bureaucratic navigation, administrative foresight, and financial sustainability. It is a decade-long endeavour so complex that it routinely eludes even seasoned corporate executives and veteran administrators. 

For an individual whose entire life has been forged outside the halls of academia, the challenge is multiplied exponentially. The vocabulary of syllabus design, faculty recruitment, accreditation frameworks, and research infrastructure is entirely foreign to those accustomed to different institutional ecosystems.

This challenge becomes uniquely pronounced when the individual tasked with building such an institution hails from a military background. The military operates on a rigid architecture of command, control, obedience, and immediate execution. Decisions are made hierarchically, and objectives are secured through absolute compliance and tactical precision. Higher education, by contrast, thrives on a completely antithetical philosophy. 

A university is built upon the principles of academic freedom, critical dissent, consensus-driven governance, and the slow, deliberate intellectual debate required to expand the boundaries of human knowledge. To transition from a culture where orders are followed without question to an environment where questioning every order is a fundamental virtue requires an extraordinary degree of intellectual agility.

The profound transformation—from a battlefield commander to the architect of an enlightened, free-thinking seat of learning—is precisely why Major General Milinda Peiris's biography, “Beyond Rank”, should be read by all

Battle-hardened soldier

This profound institutional chasm is precisely what Major General Milinda Peiris navigated when he took the helm of Sri Lanka’s premier defence academy. His remarkable journey from the battlefields to the apex of higher education administration is masterfully chronicled by his biographer, Kithsiri Amaratunga, a seasoned lecturer in English, who aptly titled it “Beyond Rank”. 

In his biographical account, Amaratunga provides an intimate look at a man who successfully bridged two vastly different worlds. To his biographer, and to those who came to understand his multifaceted character, he is simply Milinda—a name that reflects the human being behind the formidable military titles and decorations. For most of his life, Milinda was the quintessential career military officer. 

He belonged to a generation of soldiers whose youth and adulthood were entirely consumed by the grim realities of the Sri Lankan civil war. He spent decades in the field, enduring the relentless hardships of active combat, strategically planning operations, and leading troops under fire. His primary adversary was the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), a highly sophisticated militant organisation that waged a bloody, decades-long secessionist campaign to carve out a separate, independent State called Tamil Eelam in the northern and eastern provinces of Sri Lanka. 

In such an intense, high-stakes environment, where survival and national sovereignty depended entirely on martial prowess, the contemplative world of academic work is surely a luxury to a soldier moving from bunker to bunker in the battlefield.

Unquenchable academic ambitions

Beneath the camouflage uniform and the battlefield exterior, Milinda’s deep-seated academic ambitions could not be permanently obscured. His intellectual curiosity and desire to understand the deeper systemic drivers of conflict eventually led him away from the frontlines and into the sphere of rigorous postgraduate research. 

He enrolled at the prestigious Madras University in India, where he undertook a Master of Philosophy degree, while still following a course at the Indian National Defence College, focusing his research on the complex matrix of Sri Lanka’s national security challenges. This academic pursuit proved to be a profound turning point. 

As he immersed himself in the literature of political science, international relations, and strategic studies, he discovered that he possessed an equally powerful talent for academic work. He was not merely a soldier applying force; he was a scholar capable of analysing the socio-political structures that necessitated that force.

Consequently, when he was appointed as the Vice Chancellor of the newly established General Sir John Kotelawala Defence University (KDU) in 2008, he did not view the role as a comfortable pre-retirement posting or a standard bureaucratic reassignment. Instead, he willingly and enthusiastically accepted the challenge, recognising it as the perfect crucible to merge his military experience with his newfound academic passion. He understood that transforming a military academy into a fully-fledged, nationally recognised university required someone who could speak the language of both the barracks and the faculty lounge.

Foresight on sustainable peace

Though General Peiris was a seasoned soldier hardened by years in the field, he remained, above all else, an officer and a gentleman in the truest sense of the phrase. His approach to the highly volatile, real-world issues facing his fractured nation was characterised by an unyielding pragmatism and a strict commitment to rational analysis. He refused to allow emotional nationalism or rigid military dogma to cloud his judgment. This intellectual independence is starkly evident in the pioneering thesis he submitted to Madras University for his MPhil degree, appropriately titled ‘Political Reforms for Sustainable Peace in Sri Lanka’.

In this seminal work, Milinda posited an argument that was both profoundly insightful and dangerous for a serving military officer of his rank. He suggested that if Sri Lanka genuinely desired to achieve a permanent, sustainable peace rather than a temporary cessation of hostilities, the State had to adopt a sophisticated dual approach to the Tamil issue. 

This dual strategy required a simultaneous deployment of military pressure and political concessions, with an absolute, overriding emphasis placed on systemic political reforms. For this strategy to succeed, he argued, the Government of Sri Lanka had to demonstrate a genuine, transparent commitment to restructuring the State, whilst actively securing international support—most critically and controversially from India.

To fully appreciate the sheer audacity of this proposition, one must understand the political psychology of Sri Lanka at the time. In the highly polarised atmosphere of the island's ethnic conflict, suggesting a political solution that involved active Indian intervention was nothing short of anathema to the Sinhalese majority. It was a heretic suggestion that, had it been publicised widely at the time, could easily have led to him being branded a traitor to the aspirations of the nation because to speak about a political solution supported by India was anathema to many.

Anti-Indian sentiment had been deeply embedded within the Sri Lankan psyche following the deeply frustrating and traumatic experiences of the late 1980s. During that period, the Indian Government had intervened directly in the ethnic crisis, deploying the Indian Peace Keeping Force (IPKF) to the north and east of the island. The intervention was widely perceived by the majority Sinhalese population as a heavy-handed violation of national sovereignty. The subsequent escalation of violence left deep scars, and the majority community came to view India with intense suspicion, perceiving it as a regional hegemon that did not have the existential interests of the Sinhalese people at heart.

However, Milinda chose to bypass these deep-seated emotional biases. He boldly and rationally presented his argument, maintaining that sustainable peace was impossible without engaging India as a guarantor and partner.

Devolving police powers to provinces

Furthermore, Milinda’s thesis did not stop at abstract geopolitical theories; it ventured into highly specific, sensitive constitutional mechanics. He suggested that the Sri Lankan State should devolve significant autonomy to the provinces, explicitly including the devolution of police powers. This was a radical departure from the highly centralised status quo. He envisioned a sophisticated hybrid solution wherein police powers would be exercised concurrently by both the Provincial Governments and the Central Government, operating in close institutional cooperation with one another.

Within this proposed framework, he recommended that the Central Government's police forces should exclusively handle cross-border, inter-provincial crimes and national security issues, while the provincial police forces would be entirely responsible for maintaining day-to-day law and order within their respective geographical boundaries.

By any contemporary standard of military discipline and national political discourse, this was a rebellious, boundary-pushing suggestion. It was a thesis that defied the conventional hawkish positions expected from a serving high-ranking military officer who was actively fighting the very insurgency the reforms sought to address. Yet, the rational, objective man within Milinda overrode the institutional biases of his military uniform. He allowed empirical reality and political science to dictate his conclusions.

The historical events that unfolded after the dramatic end of the war in May 2009 have vindicated Milinda’s foresight. Years after the military defeat of the LTTE, the underlying questions of ethnic reconciliation, devolution, governance, and regional geopolitical balancing continue to dominate the Sri Lankan political landscape. The enduring complexity of the post-war era has proved Milinda entirely correct: a military victory can clear the ground, but only rational political reforms and strategic international partnerships can construct a lasting peace. In writing that courageous thesis, it was the rational, visionary academician within Milinda speaking.

At the helm of KDU

This rational academician was soon called upon to manifest his vision in concrete reality. The General Sir John Kotelawala Defence Academy, which had originally functioned purely as a training ground to officer cadets for the tri-forces, was formally upgraded by law to a specific defence university. 

Milinda was handed the monumental task of building it up virtually from scratch, transforming an austere training academy into a modern, comprehensive university. By conventional global standards, a defence university is expected to maintain a highly restrictive, specialised scope. It typically limits its academic footprint to faculties directly relating to the defence services—such as strategic studies, military history, and tactical engineering.

Going beyond conventional thinking, Milinda possessed a far grander, more disruptive vision. He decided that KDU should not be a cloistered military enclave, but rather a modern, expansive university housing diverse faculties that were not overtly or directly related to traditional defence work. 

In his very first address after being given the prestigious position of Vice Chancellor, he looked out at his staff and boldly declared: "I will transform this institution into an internationally recognised university." This was not empty administrative rhetoric; it was a firm, actionable manifesto. He did exactly what he promised, systematically developing an unprecedented array of diverse undergraduate and postgraduate study programs within the university structure, fundamentally altering the trajectory of the institution.

Broadening the definition of defence

To justify this unprecedented expansion, Milinda re-engineered the very philosophy of military education. He gave a much broader, modernised definition to the concept of 'defence' itself, extending it far beyond the narrow parameters of weaponry and tactics. In his vision, true national defence comprehensively covered 'civil-military relations', the 'expansion of higher education opportunities' for the populace, 'creating a professional military volunteer outfit', 'linking education with socio-economic development', and 'producing a disciplined workforce' capable of driving national progress.

These represented entirely new, progressive ideologies of developing an academic institution. By placing defence at the core but expanding the periphery, he positioned the university as a vital national instrument designed to serve the country in resolving its most burning socio-economic and structural issues. Every brick laid and every curriculum drafted under his tenure was executed precisely along these strategic lines.

Host of new faculties at KDU

The first major battleground for this expansion was the audacious project to set up a medical faculty. In the landscape of Sri Lankan higher education, establishing a medical faculty is fraught with immense political, regulatory, and financial hurdles. 

The initial challenge lay in identifying a suitable, logistically viable location and managing the massive task of establishing a state-of-the-art teaching hospital dedicated entirely to medical education. Furthermore, Milinda had to navigate the stringent demands of the Ceylon Medical Council (CMC). 

The council insisted on the provision of clinical services free of charge to the public, a necessity ensuring that medical students would have the vital opportunity to interact with and treat patients from a wide, diverse cross-section of society. From securing capital infrastructure to the meticulous selection and appointment of highly qualified professors and clinicians, the obstacles were immense. Yet, through sheer administrative willpower and meticulous planning, Milinda accomplished this task successfully, birthing a premier medical institution.

With the medical faculty established, he immediately turned his sights toward the engineering field. When this faculty was set up, he faced an identical matrix of steep challenges. He had to oversee complex staffing requirements, spearhead comprehensive curricula development, and design rigorous examinations closely tied to heavy practical, laboratory-based work. 

The overarching goal was not merely to graduate individuals with degrees, but to produce highly skilled, visionary engineers tailored specifically to meet the rapidly evolving future needs of a developing country. Through structured management and an unyielding commitment to global standards, this milestone too was successfully accomplished by Milinda.

Crucially, Milinda firmly believed that a university cannot be truly called a university if it is divorced from the culture of research. To attain this vital academic goal, he institutionalised research into defence and strategic studies, ensuring it served as the intellectual backbone of the newly emergent university. He then broke new ground by setting up a dedicated Faculty of Law. 

Rather than merely duplicating the curricula of civilian universities, Milinda introduced a unique dimension—teaching, in addition to normal civil and criminal laws, the complex legal frameworks relating to military affairs and international humanitarian law, subjects that are usually entirely neglected in the law faculties of other public universities.

His final, crowning administrative task was to set up the Faculty of Management, Humanities, and Social Sciences, thereby opening the university to the broader study of human culture, commerce, and societal dynamics. Thus, within a remarkable eight-year span of his tenure as Vice Chancellor, KDU was thoroughly transformed from a rigid training academy into a fully-fledged, multi-disciplinary university specialising in defence services.

Legacy not to be forgotten

Today, though the institution is structurally run by military personnel and maintains a distinct martial discipline, KDU possesses a remarkable, almost paradoxical spirit of generating independent, rational thought. Over the years, I have had several personal opportunities to deliver guest lectures at KDU, often speaking on sensitive subjects that were openly considered rebellious or taboo by pro-Government academia in civilian institutions. I also had the distinct opportunity to advise groups of student officers on current, highly controversial economic issues facing the island.

Without exception, though all these students had come from the strict, hierarchical backgrounds of the tri-forces, they displayed a genuine, refreshing keenness to critically look at the issues at hand, questioning status quos and debating economic data with absolute intellectual honesty. 

This vibrant, open intellectual environment is the true, enduring legacy which Milinda has left behind at KDU. It is a legacy that is currently being followed both to the letter and the spirit by his administrative successors. 

The profound transformation—from a battlefield commander to the architect of an enlightened, free-thinking seat of learning—is precisely why Major General Milinda Peiris's name remains deeply and permanently ingrained in KDU’s history.

This is the reason why his biography, “Beyond Rank”, should be read by all.

(The writer, a former Deputy Governor of the Central Bank of Sri Lanka, can be reached at waw1949@gmail.com )

title: From geography to talent: What will make nations great in the new world order? | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 5 October 2026 03:50
-     - 15

Watching the recent diplomatic spectacle surrounding President Xi Jinping in the United States prompted a simple question: what really makes a nation powerful and prosperous in the new world order? When we were young, we were taught that geography determined destiny. Later, politics and political systems were said to be decisive. Then came the argument that institutions, natural resources and economic policy mattered most. History, however, has shown that no single factor determines the destiny of a nation. Japan has few natural resources yet became one of Asia’s economic powerhouses. Australia and New Zealand prosper despite being in the southern hemisphere, challenging the old notion that prosperity was essentially a northern phenomenon. Singapore, with little land and virtually no natural resources, built one of the world’s most prosperous economies. Meanwhile, countries blessed with extraordinary natural wealth have not always converted that wealth into broad-based prosperity.

A rare diplomatic gesture: President Donald Trump personally welcomes Chinese President Xi Jinping at Joint Base Andrews — a powerful symbol of the changing dynamics of the new world order

What makes nations rich, resilient and powerful?

Increasingly, the answer is not what a country possesses, but what it can do with what it possesses. Geography is no longer enough Geography certainly matters. Access to oceans, proximity to markets, climate, natural resources and strategic location can provide enormous advantages. But geography is not destiny. Singapore transformed a difficult geographical position into a global advantage. Japan turned resource scarcity into a culture of efficiency, engineering and innovation. Switzerland built prosperity without the natural-resource endowment of many developing countries. Conversely, favourable geography can be squandered through weak institutions, poor governance and political instability. The same applies to natural resources. Resources can create wealth. Institutions determine whether that wealth creates lasting prosperity.

Talent is universal, opportunity is not

There have also been attempts to explain differences in national prosperity through racial or cultural superiority. Such explanations are simplistic and contradicted by the experience of millions of people. Consider immigrants from developing countries who have achieved remarkable success in the United States, Canada, Australia and Europe—in business, science, technology, medicine and academia. The talent was there all along. What changed was the environment in which that talent operated. This offers an important lesson for developing countries: talent is universal, but opportunity is not. Countries like companies that can identify, educate, reward and retain talent will have a tremendous advantage.

Competition creates strength

Professor Michael Porter showed that sustainable competitive advantage rarely comes from one cheap or abundant factor. Industries become stronger when they face demanding customers, intense domestic competition, high standards and constant pressure to innovate.

Italy’s footwear industry provides a useful example. Sophisticated consumers and fierce competition forced manufacturers to continually improve design, quality and efficiency. Companies that survived the demanding domestic environment were eventually able to compete internationally. The lesson is uncomfortable but important: Protection may protect an industry. Competition makes an industry stronger. Countries that permanently shield inefficient companies from competition may preserve jobs temporarily, but they risk creating industries that cannot compete globally.

Government matters—but differently

Good government is essential, but its role should not be confused with the role of business. Governments must provide the foundations: the rule of law, property rights, infrastructure, education, financial stability, predictable regulation and effective public institutions. They must also ensure competitive markets.

But governments cannot manufacture productivity.

They cannot legislate innovation.

They cannot decree entrepreneurship.

They can create the conditions in which these things flourish.

This is why leadership matters. The strongest leaders are not necessarily those who control the most institutions, but those who build institutions that continue to work after they leave office.

Productivity will decide the future

Ultimately, the wealth of nations comes down to the age old theory - productivity. A country can enjoy a temporary boom because of high commodity prices, foreign borrowing, remittances or a natural-resource discovery. Sustained prosperity is harder: it requires producing more value from every worker, every unit of capital and every hour of work. That means investing in people, technology, research and development and education.

Increasingly, it also means learning how to use artificial intelligence. The countries that benefit most from AI will not simply be those with the most powerful computers. They will be those capable of reorganising their economies, institutions and education systems around its productive use and also respecting the environment.

China, India and the new competition

China’s extraordinary transformation demonstrates what coordinated investment, infrastructure, industrial development and global integration can achieve. Its next phase will require continued gains in productivity, innovation, human capital and financial sophistication, while addressing the social and environmental consequences of rapid development. India represents a different model. Its greatest natural resource may be its people; talent pools.

Its technology sector, entrepreneurial culture, enormous domestic market and expanding pool of skilled talent provide a powerful foundation for further growth. The challenge is ensuring that prosperity becomes sufficiently broad-based and reaches beyond the major urban centres thereby reducing poverty.

The Asian Tigers offer another lesson. Their transformation was not simply the result of authoritarian government. Exports, education, infrastructure, savings, investment, disciplined economic management and integration into the global economy were critical.

Sri Lanka

For Sri Lanka, these lessons should be impossible to ignore.

We do not have China’s scale, India’s population, Japan’s industrial depth or Singapore’s strategic positioning . But we have assets that many countries would envy: an educated and entrepreneurial population, a strategic location at the crossroads of major shipping routes, a globally connected diaspora, a capable private sector and the potential to build competitive industries in services, logistics, tourism, technology and advanced manufacturing. The problem is not that Sri Lanka lacks potential. The problem is that we have repeatedly failed to convert potential into productivity. For too long, we have confused consumption with growth, short-term relief with economic reform and political promises with national strategy. Policy uncertainty, weak institutions, bureaucratic inefficiency and stop-start reforms have undermined investor confidence and discouraged long-term investment.

The next phase must be different.

Sri Lanka needs to move from an economy that seeks advantages to an economy that builds advantages.

That means investing relentlessly in human capital, technology, digital infrastructure, research and development and globally competitive businesses. It means making the country easier to invest in, easier to do business in and easier to build a career in. It means rewarding productivity and innovation rather than connections and privilege.

Education must be treated not simply as a social expenditure, but as one of the country’s most important economic investments.

Our young people should not have to leave Sri Lanka to find opportunity. If we can create an economy where talent, entrepreneurship and innovation are rewarded at home, the country’s greatest resource—the capability of its people—can become its greatest competitive advantage.

But none of this is possible without strong institutions. Sri Lanka needs predictable economic policy, fiscal discipline, an efficient and professional public service, the rule of law, competitive markets and institutions that operate independently and transparently. Sri Lanka does not need to become another Singapore. It needs to become the most productive version of itself. Our strategic location gives us an opportunity. Our people give us talent. Our diaspora gives us global connections. Our private sector gives us entrepreneurial capacity. What we need now is the institutional discipline to turn these advantages into results .

Conclusion

The world is entering a fundamentally different era. Military power will remain important. Natural resources will remain important. Geography will remain important. But increasingly, national power will also be measured by something less visible: the ability to learn, adapt and innovate. The countries that succeed will not necessarily be those with the largest populations, the most land or the greatest natural wealth. They will be those that can turn knowledge into productivity, productivity into competitiveness, competitiveness into wealth, and wealth into a better quality of life for their citizens. Therefore, countries that learn fastest, adapt fastest and invest most wisely in their people and protect their environment will be best positioned to shape the century ahead.
