title: Human edge in the age of AI: How purposeful leadership can strengthen our humanness | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 5 October 2026 03:47
-     - 14

The hidden risk: Losing our humanness

The greatest risk posed by AI is that humans are becoming increasingly machine-like.

As organisations become more data-driven, decisions may increasingly be delegated to algorithms. As systems become more efficient, individuals may be viewed primarily through metrics and dashboards. As communication becomes increasingly mediated through technology, relationships may lose depth and authenticity. This process rarely occurs intentionally. It happens incrementally, often in ways that are difficult to recognise until they become embedded in the culture of an organisation.

Over time, people may become less inclined to exercise judgement because systems provide recommendations. Responsibility may become diffused because algorithmic outputs are perceived as objective. Relationships may become increasingly transactional because digital interactions are quicker and easier than meaningful conversations. Whilst every one of these developments may appear beneficial in isolation, collectively they can alter the way we relate to ourselves, to one another and to our work.

The result is what scholars describe as mechanistic dehumanisation: a process through which people are treated like functional resources rather than human beings possessing dignity, agency and uniqueness. In organisations, mechanistic dehumanisation becomes visible when employees are viewed primarily as productivity units, when performance becomes more important than people, when algorithms replace human judgement, when compliance replaces critical thinking, when efficiency consistently takes precedence over empathy and when relationships become transactional rather than meaningful.

The danger, therefore, is not AI itself. AI is a tool. The danger lies in uncritically allowing efficiency, optimisation and standardisation to become the dominant values guiding organisational life. When this happens, organisations may become more technologically sophisticated whilst simultaneously becoming less human.

What makes us human?

If AI is increasingly capable of processing information, generating content and supporting decision-making, what remains uniquely human?

Research and lived experience suggest four fundamental qualities that distinguish us. The first is judgement. Human beings possess the ability to navigate ambiguity, competing interests and ethical dilemmas. Whilst AI can analyse data and identify patterns, it cannot exercise wisdom. It cannot determine what is right, meaningful or morally appropriate when complex human considerations are involved.

The second is agency. Human beings possess the capacity to choose, take responsibility and intentionally shape their future. AI can recommend actions and generate options, but it cannot assume ownership of decisions or accountability for their consequences.

The third is dignity. Every human being possesses intrinsic worth beyond performance, productivity or economic value. Organisations may calculate outputs and systems may rank performance, but dignity remains an inherently human concept. AI can calculate value, but it cannot recognise human worth.

The fourth is relationship. Human beings thrive through connection, belonging and shared meaning. Trust, compassion, empathy, loyalty and love emerge through relationships built over time. Technology can facilitate communication, but it cannot create genuine human connection.

These four qualities, judgement, agency, dignity and relationships, become increasingly important as AI becomes more capable. In many respects, the advance of AI makes humanness more valuable rather than less.

Purposefulness as the antidote

If mechanistic dehumanisation is the risk, purposefulness becomes a powerful response.

Purposefulness is not merely having a purpose statement, nor is it simply a matter of setting goals. Purposefulness is an ongoing process of aligning our decisions, actions and relationships with what is meaningful and life-enhancing. It involves continually reflecting on why we do what we do, how our actions contribute to human flourishing, what values we are expressing through our choices and how we can create value not only for ourselves but also for others.

In an increasingly automated world, purposefulness reconnects people with something that machines cannot provide: meaning. AI can help us determine how to do something more efficiently, but it cannot tell us why it is worth doing in the first place.

Importantly, purposefulness strengthens each of the four dimensions of humanness. It strengthens judgement by encouraging reflective thinking rather than automatic reactions. It strengthens agency by encouraging intentional action rather than passive compliance. It strengthens dignity by recognising the intrinsic worth of people beyond their utility or output. It strengthens relationships by focusing on contribution, empathy, trust and connection.

Purposefulness therefore becomes more than a personal philosophy. It becomes a practical response to the dehumanising tendencies that can accompany technological advancement.

Purposeful leadership at three levels

Purposefulness becomes most powerful when expressed through leadership. In my doctoral research, I conceptualised this through three interconnected dimensions: Purposeful Self Leadership, Purposeful People Leadership and Purposeful Organisational Leadership. 

Purposeful Self Leadership: The first responsibility of every individual is to lead themselves purposefully. This requires cultivating self-awareness, reflecting on personal purpose, understanding one’s values and intentionally developing one’s capabilities. Whilst AI can provide information, it cannot help us discover meaning. It can analyse our behaviour, but it cannot explain why we exist. It can suggest choices, but it cannot make those choices for us.

Purposeful Self Leadership therefore involves consciously embracing technology whilst refusing to become dependent upon it for our identity, values or sense of meaning. It is about developing the inner capacities that allow us to navigate life and work with intention rather than simply responding to the demands of the moment.

Purposeful People Leadership: The second responsibility of leadership is enabling others to flourish. Purposeful People Leadership focuses on developing human potential rather than merely managing performance. It involves creating environments where people feel valued and respected, where strengths are recognised and developed, where trust is cultivated, where individuals find meaning in their work and where relationships are strengthened.

Whilst AI can manage information, only leaders can inspire people. Whilst AI may help identify talent, only leaders can nurture potential. Whilst technology can optimise processes, only leaders can build trust, foster belonging and create cultures where people thrive.

Purposeful Organisational Leadership: The third responsibility is creating organisations that enable human flourishing. Purposeful organisations pursue more than profit and efficiency. They seek to create sustainable value for employees, customers, communities and society. Achieving this requires alignment between purpose, values, culture, leadership behaviours, systems and processes.

When these elements reinforce one another, organisations become places where human beings can contribute meaningfully whilst achieving collective goals. In such organisations, AI serves the purpose of the organisation rather than becoming its purpose. Technology becomes an enabler of human flourishing rather than a substitute for it.

Technology must therefore serve purpose, rather than purpose serving technology.

Human flourishing: The ultimate aspiration

The ultimate aspiration of purposefulness is human flourishing, through the pursuit of goals.

Human flourishing occurs when people are able to express their fullest potential whilst contributing positively to others and society. It encompasses meaning, growth, connection, contribution, well-being and fulfilment. Whilst performance may be one outcome of purposefulness, it becomes meaningful when it contributes to human flourishing.

From a Purposeful Leadership perspective, flourishing occurs when individuals are able to utilise both their inherited talents and their acquired talents. Inherited talents are the natural abilities, strengths and gifts with which we are born. Acquired talents are the wisdom, resilience, empathy, insight and capabilities developed through experiences, struggles and challenges.

AI may replicate patterns and generate responses, but it cannot draw meaning from suffering, transform adversity into wisdom or convert setbacks into personal growth. Human beings can. Many of the qualities we most admire in exceptional leaders have emerged not from comfort but from challenge, reflection and perseverance.

Nor can AI connect with the deeper dimensions of existence. Human beings possess a unique capacity to connect with something larger than themselves, whether understood as purpose, conscience, spirituality, higher values, service or divine energy. Throughout history, some of humanity’s greatest acts of courage, innovation, compassion and sacrifice have emerged from this deeper connection. These dimensions remain fundamentally human and cannot be replicated by machines.

What must we do?

Responding to the challenges and opportunities of AI requires action at multiple levels.

Individuals must intentionally develop self-awareness, critical thinking, emotional intelligence, human connection and purposefulness. Leaders must create cultures that strengthen judgement, dignity, trust and learning rather than merely driving efficiency. HR professionals must become custodians of human intelligence within organisations, ensuring that technology enhances rather than diminishes human capability.

Professional bodies such as CIPM have an equally important role to play. They can shape national conversations on ethical AI, human-centred workplaces, leadership development and the preservation of humanness in organisational life. Their influence extends beyond individual organisations to the broader HR profession and the future of work itself.

The responsibility also extends to public policy. Ministries responsible for labour, education, higher education, vocational education, youth affairs, sports, entrepreneurship development and the digital economy have a shared responsibility to ensure that national development strategies strengthen human capability alongside technological capability. The workforce of the future will require not only digital literacy, but also judgement, creativity, adaptability, empathy, purposefulness and ethical discernment.

The real human edge

The future will not belong to organisations that possess the power of AI. It will belong to organisations that most effectively combine artificial intelligence with human intelligence.

AI can perform many extraordinary tasks. Yet it cannot discover purpose, exercise wisdom, create genuine human connection, transform suffering into growth, experience dignity or achieve flourishing. Only people can.

Technology will undoubtedly shape the future of work. The real question is whether it will also strengthen our humanity. The value of the future will ultimately be determined by our ability to remain deeply, consciously and purposefully human.

(The author is the Managing Director and Chief Catalyst of Purposeful Leadership (Pvt) Ltd. He holds a PhD from Hult Ashridge, an MBA from the University of Sri Jayewardenepura, and is a Fellow and Gold Medallist of the Chartered Institute of Marketing, UK)

title: Budget 2027 must go looking for earnings,  not lenders: FTZMA’s thoughts for Budget 2027 | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 5 October 2026 03:43
-     - 11

The request in our Budget 2027 proposals is a practical one. Create one place that will listen. Let anyone bring an idea. Carry the credible ones through to activation. Measure honestly what the country gains, and keep opening more. Sri Lanka’s durable economic independence will be built by what it can earn, retain and reinvest, not by how much it can borrow again

By the Free Trade Zone Manufacturers’ Association

Sri Lanka’s budget is written in rupees. Its debt falls due in dollars.

That single difference sits behind most of what went wrong in 2022, and behind most of what still has to go right. It is the starting point of the proposals we have submitted for Budget 2027.

We should state our own interest at the outset. Our Association represents companies that work at the point where investment, manufacturing, exports and Government policy meet every day. Our members cannot plan, invest or employ people with confidence in an economy that keeps running short of dollars. A country that earns steadily is the only environment in which any business can operate normally. What we are asking for serves our members, and it serves every other business and household in exactly the same way.

We understand the duty of the Central Bank to protect foreign exchange liquidity, and our members comply with the rules that follow from that duty. Those rules decide how the dollars the country already has are shared out. They cannot create the next one.

Taxation cannot create a dollar

Better revenue collection and tighter spending are necessary, and that work is under way. A fiscal deficit is a shortage of rupees, and rupees can be raised at home.

The external deficit is a different problem. It is a shortage of foreign currency, and no level of taxation turns a rupee into a dollar. Those dollars can only come from what the country earns, retains or attracts from the rest of the world.

The current account has now been in deficit for four months running. In the first seven months of this year, it recorded a shortfall of 387 million dollars, against a surplus in the same period last year. One external shock was enough to move the balance by close to 1.7 billion dollars in half a year. That is how thin the base we stand on really is.

The repayment schedule for the coming decade is already fixed by contract. The earnings that will meet it are not.

Sri Lanka has never had difficulty finding lenders. Finding new earnings has been the harder task, and it is the one Budget 2027 must now take up.

Somebody, somewhere, already knows

This country has never been short of people with ideas.

A new earning path may be spotted by an exporter who sees demand her factory could serve with a small change. By an entrepreneur with a service the region would buy. By a doctor, an engineer or a researcher who knows what our skills are worth abroad. By a Sri Lankan living overseas who can see exactly what her adopted country imports and from where. By an investor weighing two locations. Or by a public officer who knows that a rule sitting in his own file is quietly stopping something worthwhile.

Ask what happens to that idea today.

Where does the person take it? Who studies it and decides whether it holds together? Who brings the four or five agencies involved into the same room? Who identifies the regulation that blocks it and asks whether that regulation is still serving its purpose? And when nobody is against it but nobody can approve it either, who owns the case until an answer is reached?

An idea with nowhere to go is the cheapest thing a country can waste.

Much attention is now going into removing what obstructs businesses that already exist. That work is necessary and long overdue. What we have asked for is the other half of the same task. No one in this country has ever been given the job of going looking for new ways to earn.

New investors look for plug and play infrastructure within and around. To support accelerated economic development investors, need integrated logistics solutions in place before they plant their machinery on the ground. It has become an urgent and high-priority action to develop necessary infrastructure for the rural EPZs such as Expressway access, water, key areas requiring immediate attention, sometime as industrial townships with all amenities

Listen, receive, activate

Our proposals ask Budget 2027 to establish one standing national mechanism that does three things.

Listen. There should be an open invitation to the whole country, and to Sri Lankans abroad, to bring forward ideas for earning or retaining foreign exchange, and to point out the rules that are preventing such activity today. A person should not need to be a large company, or a well-connected one, to be heard.

Receive. There should be a clear entry point, with a short first submission that tests the foreign exchange logic and the practical readiness of an idea. Nobody should be asked for a full business plan before anyone has told them whether the idea is worth pursuing. Most good ideas die in the paperwork long before they die on merit.

Activate. Once an idea passes that first test, a named officer should own the case, coordinate the institutions involved within fixed time limits, and carry it through to a decision. Every credible idea deserves a route to an answer, even when the answer is no.

Not everything submitted will be practical. Some proposals will need safeguards, some will need redesign, and many will be declined. We are not asking for automatic approvals, and we are not asking for another large institution. A small team with the authority to get answers out of other agencies would achieve far more than a new department with none.

What we are asking to end is the silence. An opportunity delayed for three years cannot earn, cannot learn, cannot attract investment and cannot grow. When the answer is no, the reason should be given in writing, because a written reason often reveals a rule that should itself be reconsidered.

Measure what the country actually keeps

Our proposals also ask for a common national test, which we have called Net Foreign Currency Contribution.

Gross export and investment figures can flatter. Foreign currency comes in while large amounts go straight back out again through imported inputs, equipment, overseas services, software, licence fees and finance costs. The number that matters to the country is what remains.

Net Foreign Currency Contribution asks the harder question. After the foreign currency outflows that the activity itself causes are deducted, how much did the country actually gain?

It should also count the dollars a business saves the country, for instance when a local supplier replaces an imported input. A dollar not spent abroad is worth the same as a dollar earned.

A test of this kind does more than measure. It protects the mechanism from itself, because it separates real earning from activity that only looks like earning, and it allows results to be published and checked rather than announced.

Why this matters beyond our members

Our submission includes several opportunities that we believe are ready to move. Those matter less than the point behind them, which is that no country finds its next industry by accident, and none finds it once and then stops looking.

For our members, a stronger national foreign exchange position means a predictable environment in which to invest, manufacture, employ and export. For investors deciding between Sri Lanka and somewhere else, it means a country that looks dependable. For everyone else, it means the difference between an economy that recovers and an economy that keeps having to be rescued.

The request in our Budget 2027 proposals is a practical one. Create one place that will listen. Let anyone bring an idea. Carry the credible ones through to activation. Measure honestly what the country gains, and keep opening more.

Sri Lanka’s durable economic independence will be built by what it can earn, retain and reinvest, not by how much it can borrow again.

Payment of dividends to non-resident shareholders

The country introduced a 15% dividend tax on non-resident shareholders in 2023 and a proposed tax credit scheme aims to incentivise profit reinvestment therefore in order to encourage non-resident shareholders to retain and reinvest their profits in Sri Lanka, we propose the introduction of:

The Government must prioritise infrastructure development for Free Trade Zones (FTZs) and improve internal facilities too

New investors look for plug and play infrastructure within and around. To support accelerated economic development investors, need integrated logistics solutions in place before they plant their machinery on the ground. It has become an urgent and high-priority action to develop necessary infrastructure for the rural EPZs such as Expressway access, water, key areas requiring immediate attention, sometime as industrial townships with all amenities.

We understand that the Government is planning several new EPZs as well in the coming years. We hope that Government take into consideration the above ideas when doing so and not to step in with the same blueprint of the existing traditional zones.

The existing traditional zone too needs further attention in terms of Improving external logistics and amenities plus updating, renovating and modernising the aging, dilapidated internal infrastructure. This will help expansions, reinvestments and also attracting new investments to the existing zones.

title: Solar industry at risk: New policy undermines progress on energy security | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 5 October 2026 03:40
-     - 13

Industry experts and stakeholders share their views during the panel discussion on “Affordable Clean Energy – A Right, Not a Privilege”

Sri Lanka is still in the process of recovering from an economic crisis, making energy security a critical pillar of the country’s economic stability, with the country’s electricity crisis having not yet been fully resolved. The Public Utilities Commission of Sri Lanka (PUCSL) and the National System Operator (NSO) have already warned of a serious risk of a massive electricity shortage of 450 MWh by the first half of 2027.

Today, rooftop solar power systems contribute more than 2,600 MW of capacity to the national electricity grid. Through this contribution, Sri Lanka’s local solar energy industry is estimated to save the country approximately Rs. 20.4 billion in foreign exchange each month that would otherwise be spent on imported fossil fuels. This amounts to savings of approximately Rs. 1.5 billion per day.

If the same volume of electricity had to be generated using diesel, the Government would have to spend approximately Rs. 2.5 billion per day. At a time when many countries around the world have stopped providing financing for coal-fired power plants, the absence of solar power could force Sri Lanka to once again depend heavily on diesel-generated electricity, at a staggering cost of approximately Rs. 170–180 per unit.

Against this backdrop, a recent panel discussion on “Affordable Clean Energy – A Right, Not a Privilege,” organised by the National Chamber of Commerce of Sri Lanka (NCCSL) highlighted the challenges facing the solar sector.

New policy raises concerns

The issue began with a new circular issued by the Ministry of Energy on 11 September 2026. Under the new circular, the previously successful Net Metering and Net Accounting schemes have been discontinued. Instead, all new connections and extensions of existing agreements are required to operate under the Net Plus scheme. The agreement period, which had previously been as long as 20 years, has also been reduced to a maximum of 12 years.

The financial impact on consumers is substantial. Typically, a consumer invests around Rs. 1.5 million to Rs. 2 million to install a rooftop solar system with the objective of reducing their electricity bill to zero. Under the previous system, a 5 kW system generating approximately 550 units could offset the 550 units consumed by the household, effectively bringing the electricity bill down to zero.

Under the new Net Plus scheme, however, the consumer would first sell the 550 units generated to the Government for approximately Rs. 13,000. The consumer would then have to purchase the 550 units required for household consumption from the Government at the prevailing electricity tariff, at a cost of approximately Rs. 47,000–48,000.

Receiving Rs. 13,000 and subsequently paying approximately Rs. 48,000 to purchase back the electricity generated by one’s own system is not considered a practical arrangement. With electricity tariffs in Sri Lanka increasing by approximately 5% to 7.5% annually, the policy effectively undermines the consumer’s ability to generate and use their own electricity.

Businesses face higher energy costs and reduced choice

The impact of the policy extends beyond individual consumers to businesses across the country. Businesses that could otherwise invest in rooftop solar to reduce their electricity costs and improve long-term energy security may no longer have the same opportunity to select the most economically viable energy option for their operations.

Where businesses are unable to adopt or expand rooftop solar under viable commercial arrangements, they will remain dependent on electricity purchased from the national grid. This exposes businesses to prevailing and potentially rising grid electricity tariffs, while limiting their ability to manage one of their key operating costs through investment in renewable energy.

The industry further argues that restricting consumers’ ability to choose how they generate and consume electricity raises fundamental concerns about consumer rights. It is also viewed as being inconsistent with the basic principle of least-cost electricity embodied in Sri Lanka’s Electricity Act, under which electricity supply and generation should be pursued in an economically efficient manner.

Rather than limiting access to a lower-cost renewable energy option, stakeholders argue that consumers and businesses should be allowed to select the electricity arrangement that best meets their requirements, subject to appropriate technical safeguards and grid-management requirements.

Industry questions rationale behind policy change

Authorities have justified the decision on the grounds that excessive solar capacity has already been added to the national grid and that the system must therefore be balanced.

However, the industry argues that this reasoning is contradictory. If the fundamental concern is excess electricity being added to the grid, shifting consumers to Net Plus would not resolve the issue, as electricity generated through Net Plus systems would still be fed into the national grid.

National Chamber of Commerce of Sri Lanka (NCCSL) Vice President Dr. Lakmal Fernando has alleged that the decision is the result of a conspiracy involving former Ceylon Electricity Board officials favouring diesel power plants and the so-called diesel mafia.

Instead, he proposes that if grid balancing is the concern, the solution should be to strengthen the grid rather than discourage rooftop solar. Of the approximately 33,000 transformers in Sri Lanka, batteries could be installed in the 1,000–2,000 most heavily utilised transformers to store excess solar electricity generated during the daytime and release it to the grid during the night.

Thousands of jobs and existing investments at risk

If the new policy is implemented, more than 800 companies currently operating in the solar power sector could be forced to close, potentially putting more than 21,000 jobs at risk.

The impact would extend beyond the industry itself. Approximately 166,000 consumers who have already obtained bank loans to install rooftop solar systems could also face serious financial difficulties. If a significant number of solar companies collapse, there could also be no viable industry capacity to maintain the more than 2,600 MW of solar systems already installed across the country.

Against this backdrop, NCCSL President Anura Warnakulasuriya recently wrote to President Anura Kumara Dissanayake on 23 September 2026, making two key requests.

These are to immediately revoke the Ministry directive dated 11 September and reinstate Net Metering and Net Accounting, and to make it mandatory for any future policy changes to be evaluated by the independent regulator, the Public Utilities Commission of Sri Lanka (PUCSL).

Solar industry representatives have also written to all 225 Members of Parliament to raise awareness of the issue.

Industry Proposes Alternative Solutions- Solar industry representatives have submitted a series of practical proposals to the Government aimed at protecting the sector and addressing concerns surrounding grid stability.

A key proposal is to allow consumers to select the commercial model that best suits their electricity consumption patterns, rather than making Net Plus compulsory. Consumers should be given the option of Net Metering or Net Accounting, depending on their requirements.

The industry has also proposed encouraging the use of Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) alongside solar installations. This would allow excess electricity generated during the daytime to be stored and subsequently used during periods of peak electricity demand at night, helping maintain stability across the national grid.

In addition, the national grid’s transformers and distribution networks should be upgraded to ensure that sufficient capacity is available before further rooftop solar systems are connected. The country should also move towards smart-grid technology to improve the management of distributed renewable energy.

Critical crossroads for Sri Lanka’s energy future

The industry warns that unilateral policy decisions made without independent regulation are undermining investor confidence and limiting the ability of consumers and businesses to make their own energy choices.

At a time when Sri Lanka continues to navigate economic recovery and faces potential risks to its electricity supply, stakeholders argue that protecting the country’s renewable energy capacity, maintaining consumer choice and ensuring access to least-cost electricity will be critical to long-term energy security and economic competitiveness.

Unless immediate attention is given to the concerns raised by the industry, Sri Lanka risks moving away from an energy source that can reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels and help businesses and consumers manage electricity costs, while increasing its exposure to expensive diesel-generated power.

title: The Colombo courtier: Corporate sycophancy and political power in Sri Lanka | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 5 October 2026 03:35
-     - 14

Sycophancy is insincere, excessive flattery or praise directed towards powerful, wealthy, or influential people, typically used to gain a personal advantage or favour. Essentially, it describes the behaviour of a "bootlicker" or a "toady “someone who constantly agrees with or praises an authority figure just to get a promotion, special treatment, or social status, access information, rather than out of honesty, the “yes-man” attitude

By a Special Correspondent

In the theatre of modern governance, the endless line of sycophants waiting outside a politician’s door is frequently populated not by party loyalists, but by business owners, CEOs, industry lobbyists, and prominent corporate executives. This happens when governments change, when business leaders engage with powerful politicians, sycophancy transforms from a simple survival mechanism into a highly calculated corporate strategy. By offering uncritical praise, public endorsements, and financial backing (including bribes), business leaders systematically inflate the egos of lawmakers to secure competitive advantages, regulatory relief, and lucrative state contracts at the cost of a nation.

 In Sri Lanka, the intersection of big business and political power has long driven a culture of calculated flattery. From the colonial-era, elite to modern corporate conglomerates, an endless line of business leaders has masterfully played the role of the courtier. In Colombo's high-stakes political theatre, sycophancy is a primary business strategy used to secure government contracts, tax holidays, monopolies, and favourable regulatory carve-outs for protection at the cost of competition, the poor and the SME.

 By publicly validating whichever administration holds the keys to the state, portions of the private sector intentionally insulate political leaders from economic reality. This dynamic shifts according to who is in power, operating through distinct, well-worn channels.

Post-election pivot

Sri Lankan corporate history is defined by the rapid "post-election pivot." Business tycoons who heavily financed or publicly praised an outgoing regime are frequently the first to line up at the Presidential Secretariat or Temple Trees to garland the newly elected leadership. Overnight, yesterday’s "visionary leader" is forgotten, and the new incumbent is hailed as the nation's true economic saviour. This public display of loyalty is rarely driven by ideology; it is a defensive manoeuvre to protect existing investments and ensure continuous access to state patronage and closing the doors to the masses.

The 'national development' façade - not entrepreneurs

By presenting a face of patriotic alignment with the government's "national vision," executives build personal capital, positions with key lawmakers, infiltrate into Government boards, advisory capacities and most of the time in conflicting roles collecting information and fix tenders in their favour. Corporations frequently align their corporate social responsibility (CSR) projects or major commercial investments with a politician’s personal vanity projects. Business leaders use these initiatives as tributes. Truly they are predators. Not entrepreneurs but tenderpreneurs and commission wheeler dealers.

Silent compliance and economic blind spots

When appointed to state-backed economic advisory councils, boards or trade institutions, prominent business leaders frequently choose silent compliance over rigorous dissent. During critical moments in Sri Lanka’s economic history—such as the policy decisions leading up to the 2022 economic crisis—many corporate voices remained publicly quiet or complimentary, fearing that vocal criticism would result in state retaliation, sudden tax audits, or the loss of licences. A classic case was the Gotabaya Rajapakse tax reductions in 2019 which led to the collapse of the economy. The business leaders and their chambers not only kept silent but issued statements glorifying the step towards the island’s disaster to keep the boss happy. This transactional silence creates an echo chamber where politicians genuinely believe their economic management is flawless because the country's wealthiest individuals refuse to tell them otherwise. But the funny thing is the same people are appointed to positions by every government as advisors and awarded leadership positions.

 The cost of this symbiotic relationship is ultimately borne by ordinary Sri Lankans for generations who fall into poverty and is dismantling once a promising nation into a cesspool. When the line of business leaders outside the halls of power prioritises short-term access and corporate survival over macroeconomic truth, policy errors go uncorrected and the young and able leave the country. The result is a fragile economic landscape where cronyism thrives, market competition is stifled, and governance is shaped by whoever flatters the loudest and throws the money.

title: Avishka Fernando – Another opportunity to cement his place | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 5 October 2026 02:57
-     - 6

By Sa’adi Thawfeeq

Burly, hard-hitting right-handed opening batsman Avishka Fernando gets another chance to cement his place in the Sri Lanka One-Day International side when he was recalled to the squad of 16 picked for the One-Day Tri-Series in Pakistan which also involves England.

Fernando last played for Sri Lanka in the ODI home series against Australia in February 2025. He has earned his international comeback on the back of a sensational domestic season with SSC, whom he captains.

In the Major Club Limited-Over Tournament, where SSC ended runner-up to Moors SC, Fernando finished as the leading run scorer, amassing 447 runs across seven innings, at an impressive average of 63.85, which included two centuries – notably a massive career-best 160 off 129 balls against CCC and 138 off 114 balls against Bloomfield – both scored within three days of each other in the month of September.

The only other change from the squad that toured England for the three-match ODI series is the inclusion of left-handed batting all-rounder Sahan Arachchige, who bowls off-breaks as well. 

He is fresh from leading a second string Sri Lanka side to win the Bronze medal at the Asian Games in Japan, where he starred in a crucial 93-run partnership with Tharindu Rathnayake, scoring 33 off 37 balls to guide Sri Lanka to victory against Bangladesh in the Third Place Play-off. He also showed excellent form in the 2026 Lanka Premier League, where he hit 240 runs at a strike rate of 147.23.

Fernando and Arachchige replace out-of-form Charith Asalanka and leg-spin all-rounder Wanindu Hasaranga, who is reported to be recovering from a lower back pain that cut short his tour to England. The rest of the squad retain their places from the England tour.  

Opening batsman Pathum Nissanka has been picked but will travel with the team only if he is declared medically fit. He is recovering from a strained right leg that he suffered while fielding in the third ODI against England, which resulted in him being left out of the Sri Lanka T20I squad to Pakistan.

Sri Lanka has retained their four frontline pace options in Asitha Fernando, Dushmantha Chameera, Eshan Malinga, and Dilshan Madushanka. The spin contingent comprises Maheesh Theekshana, Sachindu Colombage, and Dunith Wellalage.

Sri Lanka, who lost the bilateral ODI series to England 2-1, have a good chance to rectify that loss when they meet the same opposition twice in the One-Day Tri-Series in Pakistan conditions which will be more akin to the subcontinent pitches experienced at home.

Sri Lanka, who play the curtain-raiser match against host Pakistan on 18 October, meet England on 22 and 29 October. All matches will take place at Rawalpindi and Lahore.

title: Sri Lanka drop down to 7th in Rugby Sevens Asian ranking | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 5 October 2026 02:52
-     - 9

By Shamseer Jaleel

Sri Lanka’s hopes of ending a long wait for an Asian Games rugby sevens medal came to an end in disappointing fashion as they finished 7th in the men’s Rugby Sevens competition at the 20th Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan.

Sri Lanka entered the 12-team competition with high expectations after being ranked third in Asia not long ago. They made an impressive start to their campaign, defeating the Philippines, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), and Singapore in the group stage to qualify for the Cup quarter-finals.

However, their medal aspirations were ended by China, who edged Sri Lanka 19-12 in the quarter-final. The defeat proved costly as Sri Lanka subsequently failed to recover mentally and physically, losing to the Philippines in the playoff for fifth and sixth places despite having beaten the same opponents convincingly in the group stage.

Sri Lanka then secured seventh place with a commanding 40-5 victory over the UAE.

The final standings saw Hong Kong China take the Gold medal after defeating China, while Japan secured Bronze by beating Korea. Malaysia finished fifth, with the Philippines sixth and Sri Lanka seventh.

The result will inevitably raise questions over Sri Lanka’s preparations and coaching structure. The coaching staff was changed from Peter Woods to former national Captain Fazil Marija, but the final outcome remained much the same. The squad, led by Srinath Sooriyabandara, had trained together for more than two months and was considered a well-prepared unit.

Sri Lanka Rugby has invested considerable resources in the shorter version of the game, but consistent performances at major Asian competitions continue to remain elusive.

With the Asian Rugby Sevens second leg scheduled to be held in Colombo later this month, attention now turns to what comes next.

For Sri Lanka, the Asian Games medal dream will now have to wait another four years.

title: Each series is a build-up towards World Cups, says Kusal Mendis | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 5 October 2026 02:44
-     - 2

Sri Lanka white-ball Captain Kusal Mendis (second from right), along with teammates Chamindu Wickramasinghe, Kamindu Mendis, and Lahiru Udara, go through the customary religious rituals prior to their departure to Pakistan yesterday

White-ball Captain Kusal Mendis said that Sri Lanka was using the bilateral white-ball series and One-Day Tri-Series in Pakistan as a build-up towards the next two World Cups – the 50-over in South Africa and Zimbabwe in 2027 and the T20 in Australia and New Zealand in 2028.

“Our target is preparing for the two World Cups. We are taking every tour as practice to try out new combinations. We are looking at a squad of around 25 players for the two formats,” said Mendis prior to the team’s departure to Pakistan.

“The Pakistan tour is not easy, we have T20Is and ODIs. We have to go in with a plan. As much as we want to win, we will have to give chances to younger players and prepare a squad of at least 15 or 16 players for each format,” he said.

Sri Lanka are embarking to Pakistan on the back of series defeats in England in both formats. They were whitewashed 3-0 in the T20Is and lost 2-1 the ODI series.

“Although we lost the T20I series to England, we took a lot of positives out of it,” said Mendis. “We used new players to see how they would perform and to try and give them the experience because we are going to two World Cups. We are playing these matches with that in mind,” he added.

“The first ODI against England, we could have won as our bowlers performed very well and gave 100%. Batting was our downfall. In the second ODI, we performed excellently in all three departments and were able to win.”

Mendis said playing against pacies bowling at 140 plus was not an issue.

“Some of our top batters have faced pace of that nature and can handle them. More than the pace it is the shot selection that is important. We all make mistakes,” he said. “The pitches in England got slow and it suited us but we made a lot of mistakes and that is why we lost the series. There is no issue with extra pace; we have to learn to handle each situation. If we can do that, we can improve the number of wins.”

Sri Lanka commences their three-match T20 series with Pakistan at Rawalpindi on 9 October. [ST]

Fairfirst Insurance, Colombo Aces, and Hayleys Group ‘A’ registered wins when the 33rd Singer – MCA Super Premier League 2026 got underway on 1 October.

The Super Premier League is the Mercantile Cricket Association’s (MCA) flagship tournament, and seven star-studded teams, including a Youth Team from Sri Lanka Cricket (SLC), are vying for the Singer Trophy at the 2026 edition.

At the LLDC Ground in Kirimandala Mawatha, Fairfirst Insurance overcame BBK Partnership by eight wickets. Half-centuries from Hiran Jayasundera, Dinura Kalupahana, and Shiran Fernando followed by a four-wicket haul by Kamil Mishara and three wickets by Navod Paranavithana helped Colombo Aces defeat SLC Youth by 73 runs at the Army Ground in Dombogoda Kalutara.

At the CCC Ground, HNB ‘A,’ anchored by half tons from Anjala Bandara and Chamindu Wijesinghe, posted 294/9 in their 50 overs but were unfortunate to lose the game by 15 runs (DLS method) when the game was called off due to bad light at the end of the 36th over.
